The solution correctly identifies that a random \([n,k]\) code is MDS iff none of the \(\binom{n}{k}\) \(k\)-column subsets are linearly dependent. For each fixed subset the failure probability is asymptotically \(1/q\); with the scaling \(\frac1q\binom{n}{k}\to\lambda\) the expected number of “bad’’ subsets tends to \(\lambda\). By the Poisson limit (Stein–Chen) the count of bad subsets converges in distribution to \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)\), so the probability of having none (i.e., the code being MDS) tends to \(e^{-\lambda}\). The derivation and limit are sound, and the final answer matches the correct limiting probability.
